slides.texte_overlay:
How to stop being so
hard on yourself
Talk to yourself like you'd talk to your best friend. You'd never tell him he's useless after one mistake. Give yourself the same fair, calm voice.
Separate the mistake from who you are. "I made a bad call" is very different from "I'm a failure." One is a moment to learn from, the other is a lie.
Write down three things you did well every night. Small things count. Your brain notices failures automatically, so you have to train it to notice wins.
Compare yourself only to last year's you. Not to friends, not to people online. If you're a little better than a year ago, you're on the right track.
Give your mind something kind to do. I do five minutes a day of history, art or science, and a curious mind spends less time attacking itself.
slides.texte_sophia: I do five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. A curious mind spends far less time attacking itself.

slides.texte_overlay: Accept that progress is messy. Two steps forward, one step back is still moving forward. Expecting perfection is the fastest way to feel like a failure.
Talk to someone when the voice gets loud. A friend, a brother, a professional. Saying your thoughts out loud often shows how unfair they really are.
